item.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant policy issue affecting youth groups, with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

Scouts say they face Â£1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips

Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of Â£1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity Â£1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".

Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over Â£11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."

He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another Â£7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."

Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."

The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.

The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

item.title: ‘National scandal’: residents in England rally against surge in mega-warehouse developments
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging article on a contemporary issue affecting residents, with concrete examples and useful vocabulary.

When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen.

He had just moved into the property in Bingham, Nottinghamshire, with his wife and toddler in June.

Now, he said he was being told: “‘By the way, there’s going to be 21.5-metre-high warehouses right next to you, and there’s going to be eight of them, and you’re going to have 400 HGVs and it’s going to be a 24-hour operation’.”

He added: “I’ll be honest with you, I cried. I was so upset.”

That planning application would add to the more than 8,500 warehouses or large distribution units that have been approved across England in the past decade, fuelled by the growth of online shopping.

Analysis of official figures by the Guardian showed that almost all (95%) of the 9,009 planning applications for “megasheds” were given the go-ahead in the 10 years up to June 2026.

Of the 4,300 approved in the last five years, nearly half (1,922) were in the east, south-east and north-west of England, and 17 were in national parks, despite them having stricter rules on major developments. Six industrial developments were approved in the South Downs national park since 2021, alongside five in the North York Moors and one in the Lake District.

England’s “golden logistics triangle” – historically the Midlands area, which is within a four-hour drive of 90% of industrial developments – has expanded significantly, with the data showing that many planned developments are in newly-held Reform councils or constituencies.

Robert Jenrick, Reform MP for Newark, which Bingham falls under, met with the developer and the local council to discuss residents’ fears about the developments.

Davis closely followed events in Astley, a village in Wigan, where a public inquiry was held over towering mega-warehouses licensed to operate 24/7 being built metres from people’s homes. The powerful fightback of Astley villagers against what they described as “torture” from increased noise, light, and traffic made them figureheads in a nationwide battle against superstructures.

Davis considers them “the canary in the coal mine”.

“They’ve been so inspirational,” he added. “Seeing their videos, I was like, ‘Well, if they can do it, I think we can and I think we should.’”

Astley’s villagers had help from the Community Planning Alliance, an umbrella organisation for around 700 community groups nationwide.

Other local groups have highlighted instances where planning proposals were subtly changed or where councils cited un-evidenced demand for warehouse space. There were also suggestions that the government was not helping, after the National Planning Policy Framework, which was published in August, made it more difficult for the public to challenge planning decisions.

“The planning system is 100% biased against communities,” said Marj Powner, who runs the CPA. “We have so little power, it’s unbelievable.”

She said developers had six months to appeal a planning rejection, whereas communities had “zero, no right of appeal, none whatsoever” if an application was approved, leaving a judicial review as their only option.

“The community have six weeks to find and instruct a legal team and put together the grounds that they may have for their judicial review, and it will cost them around £60,000, which that community has to raise from donations,” she added.

Ten minutes away from Astley, residents near a 70 hectare (173 acre) site in Gibfield began their own campaign against a development that they said would tower over their homes and take away their only green space.

The development was initially backed by the Reform-led Wigan council and is managed by the Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, which is privately run by the billionaire John Whittaker. Although the developer outlined warehouses 12.5m tall, the elevated ground level put the true height closer to 15.5m, relative to their homes, residents said.

“I think there’s just this view that we’re all kind of middle-class nimbies. We’re not. We’re normal working-class people,” said Amanda Coleman, who lives in a house immediately adjacent to the site. “It’s heartbreaking.” The site is one of a number of green belt areas controversially designated as “grey belt”. While intended for previously developed land when it was introduced in 2024, a CPRE report found that 88% of grey belt approvals upon appeal were on land that had never been built on.

Protecting nature was at the heart of many of the battles different groups were embroiled in across the UK.

In Northamptonshire, campaigners spent six years fighting two mega-warehouses on a 60 hectare (150 acre) site that is adjacent to the Upper Nene Valley Gravel Pits, a legally-protected nature reserve for golden plover and lapwing birds.

Sharon Cole, who is part of a local group, Save Titchmarsh and Upper Nene Countryside and Habitats (Staunch), appealed against the planning decision on the grounds it was in breach of international law.

She said vital habitats across the UK were being destroyed through “greed” and that developers were “ looking for all the loopholes that they can find, so they can develop [land]”.

Staunch has also campaigned for the creation of an all-party parliamentary group to scrutinise the planning process.

“When I started, I truly believed that the legal system and the planning system would come good, because we knew our facts were right, and it hasn’t happened,” Cole said.

She added: “The truth’s got to come out, because this is a national scandal across the country, what is happening within the planning system. It’s going to be the ruin of our country if something doesn’t change soon.”

A North Northamptonshire council spokesperson said the council recognised “that there are a range of strongly held views” on the warehouse proposals, but could not comment on potential legal proceedings.…

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-21 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 65/100

item.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of a corporate response to a tax policy change, with some complexity but clear reporting.

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.

JP Morgan declined to comment.

item.title: COP31: Why India’s Stress on Country-led Just Transition Pathways Is Justified
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Insightful piece on climate change policy, with a focus on a developing country's perspective.

The transition away from fossil fuels must adopt a country-driven approach that suits the socio-economic realities of each nation, India said at the 31st United Nations Conference of the Parties on climate change, commonly referred to as COP31. The conference is being held in Antalya, Turkiye, during November 9-20.

“India supports the operationalization of a two-tier, Party-guided Mechanism, responsive to developing-country needs and respectful of national sovereignty and diverse national circumstances,” India’s Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said at COP31 on November 16.

This means India wants a mechanism in which global goals are set without imposing blanket, industry-wise mandates or creating new obligations. A one-size-fits-all approach won’t work, Yadav argued.

He called for just transition initiatives through a whole-of-economy and whole-of-society approach. Employment, social protection, adaptation, poverty eradication, energy access, and sustainable development are among the aspects that need to be addressed. For this, countries need to be supported with adequate finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building. These are essential to enable developing countries to implement their national priorities, he said.

Yadav’s stress on country-driven approaches is rooted in India’s reality. India’s energy transition is already advancing considerably faster than its social-protection and economic-rehabilitation arrangements.

According to an estimate by the Niti Ayog, the government’s top policy advisory body, coal mines and thermal power plants support about 1.5 million formal and informal workers, but the economic dependence goes beyond them and involves informal livelihoods across supply chains, transportation, and services concentrated in fossil-fuel dependent regions. The body said in a February 2026 report titled “Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero: Social Implications of Transition” that livelihood diversification strategies have become essential for fossil-fuel-dependent regions.

In short, India cannot afford to phase out coal too fast because that can adversely impact the socio-economic conditions of communities dependent on or around coal mines and thermal power plants.

In 2015-16, the share of thermal power, including oil and gas, stood at 210.67GW, or 69 percent of India’s 305GW installed capacity. Of this, coal accounted for 185.17 gigawatts (GW), or 61.5 percent of India’s 305GW installed capacity.

Following a decade of exponential growth in renewable energy, solar in particular, the share of fossil fuels in India’s installed capacity has slipped to 44.5 percent of its total installed capacity of 563GW. Coal’s share stood at 40 percent as of October 31, 2026.

India, the world’s second-largest coal producer, has not announced an immediate nationwide coal phase-out. Coal remains central to electricity generation. Mine closures have started accelerating nonetheless. The government has set an ambitious target of scientifically closing 147 more mines by 2028-29.

About a dozen research papers in the past five years have highlighted the negative impact of mine closures, especially on informal laborers and people living around coal mines and power plants. And the country has not yet established a comprehensive, adequately financed system in place.

An October 2026 report showed that fossil-fuel revenues from coal and petroleum resources made up 13.1 percent of own tax and non-tax revenues and 7.7 percent of total revenue receipts of Odisha. This eastern state is considered one of India’s fastest-industrializing ones.

The report, published by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, an international non-profit research and think tank organization, argued that the state’s fiscal structure’s close links to fossil fuels and extractive industries have created growing exposure to transition, market, and environmental risks.

“Given the importance of mineral royalties and coal-related revenues to the state’s non-tax income, a sustained slowdown in fossil-fuel activity could affect fiscal stability, employment, and long-term economic growth,” warned the report, titled “Sustainable Finance for a Just Transition in Odisha.” It called for a sustainable finance framework, including a dedicated transition fund.

The Council on Energy, Environment and Water, a not-for-profit policy institution and think tank based in New Delhi, published a study in March 2026. It found that 79 percent of the 700-odd respondents believed they would earn less outside coal. The survey was conducted among departmental and contractual workers in underground and opencast mines in Jharsuguda, also in Odisha.

The report, titled “Assessing India’s Coal Mine Workers: Skills, Preferences, and Future Opportunities,” showed that nearly half the workers did not want to relocate for alternative employment. About 61 percent of the respondents perceived very limited employment opportunities outside coal.

The reason is understandable. As many as 73 percent learned on the job, acquiring expertise through observation and practical experience. Only 25 percent had formal training before entering coal work.

The NITI Aayog’s report mentioned above said that over 150 districts across India are significantly dependent on fossil-fuel supply chains, directly or indirectly sustaining livelihoods for nearly one-third of India’s population.

According to their estimate, about 345,000 workers are employed in coal mines, while the informal workforce in this industry is at least twice as large, which means that over a million people are directly dependent on coal mining. The report says that approximately 178,000 formal mining jobs could be affected by 2030. At least twice as many informal jobs could be potentially affected.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 02:53 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/cop31-why-indias-stress-on-country-led-just-transition-pathways-is-justified/

item.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Update on the situation in Ukraine, with a focus on European leaders' stance.

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.…
